figures.caption: Figure 1. Comparison of HF-scavenging reaction enthalpies of simple metal oxides (MxO1/2 where M is an alkali or alkaline-earth metal, Al or Zn) calculated by DFT (Equation (5)) with the experimental enthalpies calculated using available thermochemical data (Equation (6)). Using DFT energies for HF and H2O results in an excellent agreement with experiment, obviating the need for energy corrections for molecules. The error-bars show combined standard uncertainties (CSU) in experimental values. The dashed-lines show the enthalpy limit dH_s-HF[Li2O], below which voltage of MxF is always higher than the corresponding MxO1/2. The dotted-line represents perfect agreement with experiment.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Comparison of HF-scavenging reaction enthalpies of p- and d-block metal oxides calculated by DFT (Equation (5)) with the experimental enthalpies calculated using available thermochemical data (Equation (6)). The error-bars show combined standard uncertainties (CSU) in experimental values. The superscript 'a' denotes values listed in thermochemical tables, 'b' denotes ref. [78,79] and 'c' denotes ref. [80,81]. M2.67+ corresponds to M3O4 reacting with HF to produce MF2 and MF3. BeO is also included in this plot. The dashed-line represents perfect agreement with experiment.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Calculated average voltages for oxides and ﬂ uorides versus voltages estimated from experimental formation enthalpies. Voltages for oxides and ﬂ uorides correspond to conversion reactions M O Li M 1/2Li O 1/2 2 x x + → + and M F Li M LiF x x + → + , respectively, and they are calculated as described in Equations ( 9–13) . The error-bars show combined standard uncertainties (CSU) in experimental values.

Figure 4. DFT average lithiation voltages of s-, p- and d-block metal oxides and ﬂ uorides, via the conversion reactions of the form x x M O Li M 1/2Li O 1/2 2 + → + and M F Li M LiF x x + → + , respectively. The dashed-line is an arbitrary discharge cutoff voltage (i.e., the lowest voltage attained during the discharge) of 3.0 V for a sample cathode to be coated. If a prospective coating for this sample cathode has a lithiation voltage lower than the discharge cutoff of the cathode (i.e., the components of the coating lie in the window enclosed by the dashed-lines), the coating will not tend to absorb lithium.

Figure 5. The design chart for comparing HF-scavenging tendencies of oxides ( s HF H −Δ −), lithiation voltages of their corresponding ﬂ uorides relative to an arbitrary discharge cutoff of 3.0 V ( 3.0 M F V x − ), Ω V and Ω G of 81 metal-oxide coating candidates for Li-ion battery cathodes. Compounds are labeled with their cations for simplicity. Sample property rectangles are drawn for Al 3+ and Mg 2+ . Such a rectangle for a material shows that it is thermodynami- cally a better coating than materials that remain inside.

Figure 6. Coating candidates that pass the applied screens versus their normalized HF-scavenging capacities. Averages of the normalized scav- enging capacities are also shown. Compounds are labeled with their cations for simplicity.
